content: An unblinded randomized trial demonstrated that children at high risk for skin cancers who used sunscreen developed fewer nevi compared to those who did not use sunscreen. However, several epidemiologic studies have reported a higher risk of melanoma among sunscreen users compared to non-users. A recent meta-analysis of population-based case-control studies found no significant effect of sunscreen use on melanoma risk. These conflicting results may be attributed to the fact that sunscreen use is more prevalent among fair-skinned individuals, who are inherently at higher risk for melanoma, compared to darker-skinned individuals. Alternatively, the findings may suggest that sunscreen use could potentially be harmful if it encourages prolonged sun exposure without providing complete protection against carcinogenic radiation. The only evidence supporting the effectiveness of skin self-examination comes from a single case-control study, although the definition of self-examination in this study was limited. This study did not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that skin self-examination reduces melanoma incidence or improves melanoma outcomes. Community and workplace educational interventions have been shown to effectively increase the use of skin protection measures, such as wearing hats, long-sleeve shirts, and seeking shade. However, evidence regarding the effectiveness of clinician counseling to prevent skin cancer is extremely limited. Most studies on counseling have focused on intermediate outcomes, such as knowledge and attitudes, rather than actual behavioral changes. In a recent survey, 60% of pediatricians reported that they usually or always counsel patients about skin protection. However, advice to use sunscreen is more commonly given than advice to wear protective clothing or avoid midday sun exposure. Simple reminders and instructional materials for clinicians can help address some barriers to regular counseling. A randomized trial of a community-based intervention involving 10 towns in New Hampshire suggested that office-based counseling by physicians may be an effective component of a multimodal program to promote skin protection. In the intervention towns, the proportion of children using some form of sun protection increased significantly (from 78% to 87%), compared to a decrease in the control communities (from 85% to 80%). More parents in the intervention towns reported receiving sun protection information from a clinician. However, most of the observed change was attributed to increased sunscreen use rather than reduced sun exposure. There is limited data regarding the potential harms of counseling or specific skin protection behaviors.
